title: The women of N'jau who turned plastic bags into purses
person: Isatou Ceesay and the women of N'jau
status_note: Ceesay was speaking publicly about her work in September 2023 (News On AIR) and Worldcrunch reported new projects in August 2024. Sources give slightly different start dates (1997 in ISEP's interview; 1998 in News On AIR); 1997 is used here.
summary: In a Gambian village with no rubbish collection, Isatou Ceesay and a handful of women began crocheting discarded plastic bags into purses to sell, creating income and cleaner streets.
small_thing: Ceesay called a meeting in N'jau to talk about recycling plastic, and only five women came. With them she began washing discarded plastic bags, cutting them into strips and crocheting them into small purses.
problem_text: Plastic bags had replaced traditional baskets in N'jau, and with no regular rubbish collection they piled up in streets and behind homes. Rainwater collected in discarded bags and bred mosquitoes, goats died after eating plastic, and people burned plastic as fuel, releasing toxic fumes.
why_started: Ceesay grew up in a poor family whose father had come to The Gambia as a refugee from Mali, and she was looking for a way to earn money (Worldcrunch). She was also troubled by the harm plastic was doing in her village; she told ISEP that a Peace Corps volunteer showed her that old bags could be turned into yarn, and her sister had already taught her to weave.
what_they_did:
Starting in 1997, the group washed and dried plastic bags, cut them into long strands of plastic yarn and crocheted them into coin purses, later adding other items such as pen holders, balls and necklaces (ISEP). Ceesay told ISEP she could make about two and a half purses a day. The group sold the goods at local markets.

According to Worldcrunch, the work grew into the Women's Initiative Gambia, an NGO Ceesay leads, which trained local women who collected materials from dumps. She has since started projects making charcoal from organic waste and sanitary pads from sustainable materials.
what_changed: Worldcrunch reported in 2024 that about 350 women from her village earn an income through the movement, and ISEP reported that the Gambian Women's Initiative had more than 11,900 members at its last count. In 2012 Ceesay received an award from the International Alliance for Women (Worldcrunch). Her story became the 2015 children's picture book One Plastic Bag. The amount of plastic diverted from the environment has not been independently measured.
what_they_learned: Ceesay has said that many people doubted her at first and did not take her seriously, and that training women directly mattered because some men wanted their wives to stay dependent on them.

quote.text: I informed the whole community, but only five women answered my call.
quote.speaker: Isatou Ceesay

why_it_matters: Crocheting old bags into purses will not end plastic pollution in The Gambia. But the N'jau group shows how a waste problem can be turned into a small, steady income for women, and how a handful of people can start a local habit of collecting rubbish rather than burning it.
setbacks: Only five women answered the first call, and others ridiculed the effort as a waste of time (ISEP). Ceesay told Worldcrunch that many people expected her to fail and that some men opposed their wives taking part. ISEP also noted that middlemen setting prices limited what women earned.

copy_this.problem: Thin plastic carrier bags littering streets and fields with no collection service.
copy_this.what: Collect, wash and dry used plastic bags, cut them into strips ('plarn') and crochet or weave them into useful items to sell or use.
copy_this.materials: Used plastic bags, water and soap, scissors, crochet hooks.
copy_this.skills: Basic crochet or weaving, which can be taught in a few sessions; simple bookkeeping if selling.
copy_this.time: Each item takes several hours by hand; groups often meet weekly.
copy_this.people: Can start with one person; a small group of five to ten makes collection and selling easier.
copy_this.risks: Handle dirty plastic with care and wash hands; never burn plastic offcuts. Hand-made items earn modest income, so be honest with members about earnings.
copy_this.adapt: Use whatever waste is abundant locally (rice sacks, tyres, food wrappers), and link with local markets, schools or tourist outlets for sales.
copy_this.lessons: Start small with people who are willing, and expect scepticism. Agree fair prices among members so middlemen do not take most of the value.

title: A backyard lab that turns Nairobi's plastic into paving stones
person: Nzambi Matee (Gjenge Makers)
status_note: Most recent independent reporting found (Unbias the News, 2023; Africanews page updated 2024) describes the business as operating. Current output was not independently confirmed for 2025–2026.
summary: Kenyan engineer Nzambi Matee left her job, set up a lab in her mother's back yard and developed paving blocks made from waste plastic mixed with sand.
small_thing: In 2017 Matee left her job and set up a small laboratory in her mother's back yard in Nairobi to experiment with mixing waste plastic and sand.
problem_text: Plastic bags and packaging litter Nairobi's streets, and only around a tenth of plastic in Kenya is recycled, according to Africanews. Kenya banned single-use plastic bags in 2017, but Unbias the News reports the ban has not been fully effective and many other plastics are not covered.
why_started: UNEP reports that Matee, who studied materials science and had worked as an engineer in Kenya's oil industry, was moved to act after routinely seeing plastic bags strewn along Nairobi's streets. She told UNEP she put all her savings into the project in its first year.
what_they_did:
Gjenge Makers shreds plastic waste, mixes it with sand, heats it and compresses it into paving blocks using a locally built machine (Unbias the News). A social entrepreneurship scholarship to the University of Colorado Boulder let her use materials labs to refine the plastic-to-sand ratios (UNEP). The pavers are certified by the Kenya Bureau of Standards, according to UNEP.

The blocks are used on paths, alleys and school grounds; UNEP reported that a skills training centre in Mukuru Kyaba, an informal settlement, laid them where pupils had previously walked on dirt paths.
what_changed: UNEP reported production of about 1,500 pavers a day in 2020. Unbias the News reported in 2023 that the company processed 10 to 20 tonnes of plastic waste a month, and Africanews reported 50 tonnes recycled in 2021 and more than 100 direct and indirect jobs. Claims that the pavers are stronger and cheaper than concrete come from the company and, as Unbias the News notes, have not been independently verified. Matee was named a UNEP Young Champion of the Earth in 2020.
what_they_learned: Matee has said demand is higher than her equipment can meet, and that scaling up from one paver to thousands is the real challenge. She has said she is willing to license the technology so others can use it.

quote.text: Plastic is a material that is misused and misunderstood.

why_it_matters: Paving blocks will not absorb all of Nairobi's plastic waste, and the long-term behaviour of plastic-based building materials still needs independent study. But the project shows how locally built machinery and local waste can be turned into a product people need, while creating jobs.
setbacks: Matee told UNEP the first full batch took years of work, and that she gave up her social life and savings for a year. Neighbours complained about smells from her early experiments, and in 2023 she said demand exceeded her production capacity (Unbias the News).

copy_this.problem: Mixed plastic waste with little recycling market.
copy_this.what: Explore turning sorted waste plastic into practical building products, ideally by partnering with an existing producer or licensing a proven process rather than starting from scratch.
copy_this.materials: Sorted, cleaned plastic; sand; shredder, heating and moulding or pressing equipment.
copy_this.skills: Materials testing, machine building or operation, workplace safety, product certification.
copy_this.time: Years of development for a new product; Matee's prototyping took around a year and the first full batch longer.
copy_this.people: A small technical team, plus waste collectors and buyers.
copy_this.risks: Heating plastic can release harmful fumes; work only with proper ventilation, protective equipment and expert advice. Products used in building need testing and certification. Possible microplastic shedding over time is not well studied.
copy_this.adapt: Smaller groups can start by collecting and sorting plastic for an existing recycler or brick-maker.
copy_this.lessons: Get products tested to national standards early, and plan for the jump from making one item to making thousands.

title: Cargo bikes and reward points for recycling in Lagos
person: Bilikiss Adebiyi-Abiola (Wecyclers)
status_note: Africanews reported Wecyclers operating in Lagos in November 2022 (page updated 2024). No independent 2025–2026 report was found; current scale not confirmed.
summary: Wecyclers sends riders on cargo tricycles into low-income Lagos neighbourhoods to collect recyclables, rewarding households with points they can swap for food, goods or cash.
small_thing: As an MBA student, Adebiyi-Abiola first tested the idea of residents dropping recyclables at kiosks. When a survey showed that was inconvenient, the team switched to collecting from doorsteps by bicycle.
problem_text: Lagos produces around 10,000 tonnes or more of waste a day, and only about 40% is collected, according to figures reported by AFP and Al Jazeera. Rubbish blocks gutters, contributing to flooding, mosquitoes and malaria, and rubbish trucks cannot reach many unpaved streets.
why_started: Adebiyi-Abiola grew up in Lagos and saw plastic and aluminium waste pile up in streets and gutters (MIT News). The idea took shape in 2010 during a development ventures course at MIT, and she launched Wecyclers in 2012 with fellow MBA student Alexandra Fallon.
what_they_did:
Locally employed riders use human-powered cargo tricycles, designed with help from MIT D-Lab and built by local craftspeople, to collect recyclables door to door. Materials are weighed and subscribers receive points by text message for each kilogram, which they can exchange for household goods, phone credit or cash (MIT News; AFP).

The materials are sorted and sold to recycling factories, which make products such as pillow stuffing and flip-flops. AFP reported that the Lagos Waste Management Authority (LAWMA) backed the scheme and loaned a sorting site.
what_changed: According to MIT News in 2015, Wecyclers had collected more than 600 tons of recyclables from over 6,500 households and created 75 jobs. Al Jazeera reported in 2019 that about 60% of its employees were women and that it had won the King Baudouin Foundation's African Development Prize. Africanews reported in 2022 that it continued to employ low-income residents as sorters and riders. These figures come from the organisation's own statements as reported by the media; the overall effect on Lagos's waste has not been independently measured.
what_they_learned: Adebiyi-Abiola has said that for many poor households recycling first seemed a luxury, since survival comes first, so rewards were a way to start the conversation and show that recycling could help people earn.

quote.text: We want to empower people to use recycling as a way to work out of poverty.

why_it_matters: A fleet of cargo bikes cannot fix a megacity's waste system on its own. But Wecyclers shows how a simple incentive and low-cost transport can reach streets that trucks miss, and how waste can become a source of income in low-income neighbourhoods.
setbacks: The first kiosk model failed because residents found it inconvenient, and an early bicycle-and-wagon design was too hard to pedal (MIT News). Adebiyi-Abiola told Al Jazeera she faced sexist comments as a woman running a waste business.

copy_this.problem: Recyclables are not collected from neighbourhoods that bin lorries cannot reach.
copy_this.what: Run a door-to-door collection round on bikes or carts, weigh what each household gives and reward them in points, goods or cash, then sell sorted materials to recyclers.
copy_this.materials: Cargo bikes or handcarts, sacks, a scale, a simple record system (paper or phone), a sorting space.
copy_this.skills: Route planning, record keeping, finding buyers for sorted materials, building trust with residents.
copy_this.time: A few hours a week for a pilot street; full-time for a business.
copy_this.people: A small team of riders and sorters, plus a coordinator.
copy_this.risks: Prices for recyclables rise and fall; rewards must be affordable. Provide gloves and safe working conditions for collectors.
copy_this.adapt: Start with one material that has a reliable buyer, such as plastic bottles or cans, and one neighbourhood. Ask residents what is convenient before designing the service.
copy_this.lessons: Survey people first; Wecyclers dropped its original idea when residents said it did not suit them.

title: Niger's farmers who let the trees grow back
person: Farmers of Maradi and Zinder, with agronomist Tony Rinaudo
status_note: Tony Rinaudo is alive and was still promoting the practice in late 2024 (World Vision, December 2024). The practice continues among farmers in Niger and has spread to other countries.
summary: In southern Niger, farmers began protecting and pruning tree stumps that resprouted in their fields, regreening millions of hectares of farmland at very low cost.
small_thing: Instead of clearing every shoot from their fields, farmers chose a few stems growing from old tree stumps, pruned them and protected them so they could grow back into trees.
problem_text: By the 1970s and 1980s much of the farmland in southern Niger had been stripped of trees. Farmers there described sand covering their crops, poor yields and a shortage of firewood (Farm Radio International).
why_started: Tony Rinaudo, an Australian agronomist working with a mission organisation in Niger from 1981, realised in 1983 that many low 'bushes' in farmers' fields were in fact trees regrowing from living root systems (Right Livelihood). Working with farmers in the Maradi area, he encouraged them to protect this regrowth rather than plant new trees, which had often failed.
what_they_did:
Farmer-managed natural regeneration (FMNR) means surveying a field, choosing a few healthy stems of useful local species from each stump, cutting the rest for fodder or mulch, pruning the chosen stems and protecting them, and repeating this every few months (Right Livelihood). During the 1984 famine a food-for-work programme introduced the method to about 70,000 people.

In villages such as Dan Saga in Aguié district, farmers' groups set community rules to protect regrowing trees, with committees of men and women monitoring them and a village-run wood market sharing the income (Farm Radio International).
what_changed: Researchers including Chris Reij report that farmers in Niger's Maradi and Zinder regions have applied FMNR on 4.2 million hectares (Cotillon, Tappan and Reij, 2021). Right Livelihood puts restored land in Niger at about 5 million hectares with over 200 million trees. In Dan Saga, a farmer leader reported millet yields rising several-fold and wood sales helping families through the 1999–2000 food crisis (Farm Radio International). Rinaudo received the Right Livelihood Award in 2018; the spread of the practice is attributed to farmers themselves as much as to him.
what_they_learned: Rinaudo has said that the 'underground forest' of living roots was there all along: he had seen the bushes many times without realising their significance. Working with nature and with farmers' own choices proved cheaper than tree planting.

quote.text: If you work with nature, miracles are possible.
quote.speaker: Tony Rinaudo

why_it_matters: Letting trees regrow in fields will not by itself end hunger or drought in the Sahel. But FMNR shows how farmers can restore soil, shade and fuel on their own land at very low cost, using knowledge and roots that are already there.
setbacks: Early on, farmers saw trees as competing with crops, and protecting regrowth depended on community rules being followed (Farm Radio International). Earlier tree-planting efforts in the region had largely failed.

copy_this.problem: Degraded farmland with few trees, poor soil and scarce firewood.
copy_this.what: Look for living stumps and root sprouts in fields, choose a few strong stems per stump, prune and protect them, and keep pruning every few months.
copy_this.materials: A cutting tool, markers (paint or cloth strips) for protected stems, local agreements to keep livestock and cutters away.
copy_this.skills: Recognising useful local tree species; basic pruning. Neighbour farmers can teach each other.
copy_this.time: A few days per field each year; benefits build over several seasons.
copy_this.people: One farmer can start; it works best when a whole village agrees on rules.
copy_this.risks: Too many trees can shade crops, so thin and prune. Agree rules on cutting and grazing to avoid conflict between neighbours.
copy_this.adapt: Works in many drylands where tree roots survive. Combine with mulching and existing farming practices; seek local extension or NGO advice.
copy_this.lessons: Build on what farmers already have rather than bringing in seedlings, and make sure the people who protect the trees benefit from them.

title: A teenager's scrap-metal windmill in rural Malawi
person: William Kamkwamba
status_note: Kamkwamba is alive and in September 2025 was leading the Moving Windmills Project in Malawi (Gulf News). Coordinates are for Kasungu town, the nearest town centre; the famine is dated 2001 in some sources and 2002 in others.
occupation: student (at the time); now engineer and innovator
summary: After famine forced him out of school, 14-year-old William Kamkwamba used a library book and scrap parts to build a windmill that brought electric light to his family's home.
small_thing: Unable to afford school fees, Kamkwamba borrowed science books from a small local library, including one called Using Energy, and began collecting scrap to build a wind turbine.
problem_text: Like most rural households in Malawi at the time, the Kamkwamba family had no electricity. During the famine of the early 2000s the family could not afford food or school fees, and William dropped out of school (Gulf News; Snopes).
why_started: Kamkwamba was thinking about how to get electricity at home, and found a book on energy in the village library (Wall Street Journal; Gulf News). He built the windmill at around 14 years old.
what_they_did:
He built a tower from blue-gum tree trunks, blades from flattened plastic pipes and a turbine from bicycle parts (Wall Street Journal). The windmill powered lights and a radio in the family home; by 2007 the family's setup ran light bulbs, a TV and a radio. A later windmill powered a water pump to irrigate crops during drought (Snopes, citing Malawi's Daily Times).

His story became the memoir The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind (2009) and a Netflix film. He went on to the African Leadership Academy and Dartmouth College, graduating in 2014.
what_changed: The family gained electric light and, later, water for irrigation. His mother told the Wall Street Journal that people first laughed at him and that their lives were much happier afterwards. Through the Moving Windmills Project, he now works on education, agriculture and sustainability in Malawi and plans an innovation centre for young people (Gulf News, 2025). Wider community impact has not been independently measured.
what_they_learned: Kamkwamba has told audiences that challenges are inevitable when starting out, and that young people should not let them stop them from pursuing their goals.

quote.text: I got information about a windmill, and I try and I made it.

why_it_matters: One home-made windmill does not solve energy poverty. But Kamkwamba's story shows how curiosity, a library and salvaged materials can bring small-scale renewable power to a household, and it has encouraged many young people to try practical problem-solving.
setbacks: He had to leave school because of the famine, and neighbours initially laughed at his project (Wall Street Journal). He has said he faced many challenges when he started.

copy_this.problem: No electricity for basic lighting, phone charging or a radio.
copy_this.what: Learn how small wind or solar systems work and, with supervision, build a simple demonstration turbine; for daily use, consider proven small solar kits.
copy_this.materials: Library or online guides, salvaged bicycle parts, a small dynamo or generator, wood or metal for a tower, wiring, a battery.
copy_this.skills: Basic mechanics and electrics; patience for trial and error.
copy_this.time: Weeks to months for a first working model.
copy_this.people: One person can start; a teacher, mentor or school club helps.
copy_this.risks: Tall towers can fall and spinning blades can injure; electrical wiring and batteries can cause shocks or fires. Always work with an experienced adult or technician.
copy_this.adapt: Schools and youth clubs can run small renewable energy projects; communities can pool resources for a shared charging point.
copy_this.lessons: Start with what is available, keep learning from books and others, and expect early doubts from people around you.

title: Birthday Trees: a Ugandan teenager's way to replant forests
person: Leah Namugerwa
status_note: In April 2024 UN-Habitat listed her as a 19-year-old climate and child rights activist serving on its Youth Advisory Board. Tree-planting totals after 2021 were not independently confirmed. She lives in the Kampala area (Mukono); planting has included a forest in Entebbe.
summary: Ugandan teenager Leah Namugerwa marked her 15th birthday by planting 200 trees, then started Birthday Trees, inviting others to celebrate birthdays by planting trees.
small_thing: For her 15th birthday in 2019, instead of a party, Namugerwa planted 200 trees and offered trees to others to plant on their own birthdays.
problem_text: Uganda's forest cover has fallen sharply since the 1990s, from about 24% to 8% according to figures reported by Africanews. Plastic bag litter was also a concern; Namugerwa linked plastic bags to cholera in Kampala's informal settlements (UN-Habitat).
why_started: Namugerwa began campaigning against plastic bags in 2018 and, inspired by Greta Thunberg, started striking alone for the climate on 1 February 2019 (UN-Habitat). She told reporters she set up Birthday Trees as a way of restoring Uganda's lost forest cover.
what_they_did: Namugerwa planted 200 trees for her 15th birthday and 500 for her 16th, and plants trees on behalf of people who want to mark their birthdays this way (Africanews). Alongside this she helped lead Fridays for Future activities in Uganda, including weekly strikes, lakeshore clean-ups and school awareness work, and petitioned for a ban on plastic bags (UN-Habitat; Africanews).
what_changed: Africanews reported in 2021 that she aimed to plant one million trees and that people in other countries had taken up the birthday idea; she said she had been joined by others, including a young woman who found her on social media. She was named one of UN-Habitat's youth delegates in 2019 and later joined its Youth Advisory Board. The survival rate of the trees planted has not been independently measured.
what_they_learned: Namugerwa has said that each time she plants trees, more people come to help, and that her father supported her decision from the start.

quote.text: I celebrated my birthday in 2019 by planting 200 trees.

why_it_matters: A few hundred trees a year will not reverse Uganda's forest loss. But tying tree planting to birthdays turns a personal celebration into a repeatable act that friends and strangers can copy, and it shows how young people can start local restoration without waiting for permission.
setbacks: She began her climate strikes alone, and in 2019 she was unable to attend the UN Youth Climate Summit because her visa did not arrive in time (UN-Habitat). Her one-million-tree goal was described in 2021 as still a long way off (Africanews).

copy_this.problem: Local tree loss and few chances for young people to take part in restoration.
copy_this.what: Mark birthdays or other milestones by planting native trees, and invite friends and family to do the same.
copy_this.materials: Native seedlings from a local nursery or forestry office, spades, water, stakes or guards, permission for the planting site.
copy_this.skills: Basic planting and aftercare; knowledge of suitable local species (ask a nursery or forestry officer).
copy_this.time: A morning to plant; regular watering and checks for the first year or two.
copy_this.people: One person can start; a school, faith group or youth club can sustain it.
copy_this.risks: Planting the wrong species or in the wrong place can harm ecosystems; get landowner and local authority permission and follow local advice. Many seedlings die without aftercare.
copy_this.adapt: Plant for weddings, graduations or memorials; partner with a school to look after the trees.
copy_this.lessons: Count trees that survive, not just trees planted, and make it easy for others to join.

title: A lawyer and his neighbour start clearing a Mumbai beach
person: Afroz Shah
status_note: Weekend clean-ups at Versova were briefly suspended in the clean-up's second year after harassment of volunteers and uncollected waste, then resumed. The Better India reported a large volunteer clean-up at Versova in February 2026.
summary: Mumbai lawyer Afroz Shah and an elderly neighbour began picking up rubbish on Versova Beach in 2015; weekly volunteer clean-ups grew into a long-running citizen movement.
small_thing: In 2015 Afroz Shah and his 84-year-old neighbour, Harbansh Mathur, went down to Versova Beach and started picking up the plastic and rubbish themselves.
problem_text: Versova Beach in Mumbai runs for about 2.5 km. By 2015 it was covered in plastic bags, sacks, bottles, clothes and shoes; UN Environment reported litter shin-deep in places. Much of it was washed in by the sea and creeks or dumped from nearby settlements.
why_started: Shah had grown up in Versova and remembered a beach without rubbish. Returning in 2015, he could see heaps of plastic from his flat and, according to Al Jazeera, described the garbage as five feet high. He shared his shock with his elderly neighbour and the two began clearing it.
what_they_did:
Shah and Mathur began clearing the beach by hand. Shah then went door to door to residents and fishing families, explaining how marine litter harms the ocean and asking them to join. Volunteers came every weekend, working with their hands alongside hired tractors and an excavator, and the collected waste was sent on for recycling.

Al Jazeera reported that Shah paid for much of the work himself. He also raised concerns about the lack of toilets in nearby settlements, which he linked to the condition of the beach.
what_changed: UN Environment described the effort as the world's largest beach clean-up, reporting more than 500 volunteers and around two million kilograms of waste removed within its first year; by the time Shah won the UN's Champions of the Earth award in December 2016, UNEP put the total at 4,000 tonnes. Al Jazeera reported in 2018 that the team had removed more than 13 million kg, and that nearly 100 olive ridley turtle hatchlings were seen heading to the sea at Versova in March 2018, which it described as the first such hatching there in about two decades. These figures come from the organisers and media reports; the long-term ecological impact has not been independently measured.
what_they_learned: Shah has stressed that pollution is a shared responsibility rather than only the government's, telling Al Jazeera: "But the government is not littering, we are."

quote.text: We humans need to reignite our bond with the ocean and we don't have to wait for anybody else to help us do that.

why_it_matters: Clearing one beach does not stop plastic entering the ocean upstream. But the Versova clean-up shows how persistent, local volunteering can change a neglected public space and draw attention to waste collection and sanitation gaps that need wider action.
setbacks: Volunteers were heckled and intimidated on the beach, and municipal trucks did not always remove the rubbish they collected. Shah briefly suspended the clean-up after about two years; it resumed after the Maharashtra Chief Minister asked him to continue and directed the civic administration to clear the beach (Al Jazeera). His co-founder Harbansh Mathur died in 2016.

copy_this.problem: Litter on a local beach, riverbank or public green space.
copy_this.what: Organise a regular, same-time-every-week clean-up and invite neighbours, shopkeepers and fishing or boating families to join.
copy_this.materials: Gloves, sturdy sacks, litter pickers, first-aid kit, water; arrangements with the local council for waste collection.
copy_this.skills: Basic organising, talking to neighbours, coordinating with the local authority.
copy_this.time: A few hours each week, kept up over months.
copy_this.people: Start with two; aim to grow through word of mouth.
copy_this.risks: Sharp objects, medical or hazardous waste, tides and heat. Agree collection with the council first so bags are not left behind, and plan for volunteer safety.
copy_this.adapt: Works for rivers, parks and streets; pair clean-ups with conversations about where the waste comes from.
copy_this.lessons: Consistency builds trust; collected waste must be taken away promptly; long-term change needs waste services and sanitation, not volunteers alone.

title: The teenager who began planting bamboo on a bare sandbar
person: Jadav Payeng
status_note: Payeng was publicly active in November 2025. In late 2025 a fire, which officials attributed to arson, destroyed more than 5,500 saplings in a newer section planted in 2022 (Outlook Traveller, January 2026).
summary: Since 1979 Jadav Payeng has planted and tended trees on an eroded Brahmaputra sandbar in Assam, growing a forest now known as Molai.
small_thing: As a teenager in 1979 Payeng was given a few bamboo plants and began planting them on a bare sandbar in the Brahmaputra.
problem_text: River erosion along the Brahmaputra in Assam had cut off and stripped islands to bare sand. After the 1979 floods, the sandbar near Payeng's home offered no shade or habitat, and wildlife died on the exposed sand.
why_started: After floods in 1979, Payeng saw dead snakes on the hot, shadeless sand. He told NPR the sight made him think that humans too could die in such heat, and he began planting.
what_they_did:
Payeng began with bamboo and other native, low-value plants, and later added trees such as teak. Al Jazeera reported that he planted banana trees to feed wild elephants and keep them from straying into villages. He tended the forest alongside his family's dairy work, delivering milk each morning before going to plant.

In recent years he has spoken widely on tree planting in schools and, according to a 2023 PTI report, has worked with a team of about 50 people planting on a much larger area of Majuli river island.
what_changed: Al Jazeera reported in 2014 that the forest covered about 550 hectares and supported wild elephants, tigers, rhinos and deer; NPR (2017) gave a figure of about 1,300 acres. These figures come from media reports rather than a published survey. Payeng has received India's Padma Shri civilian award.
what_they_learned: Payeng has said he sees nature as sacred and gives it as his inspiration; he argues that tree planting should be taught in schools everywhere.

quote.text: When I saw it, I thought even we humans will have to die this way in the heat.

why_it_matters: One forest cannot reverse regional deforestation or river erosion. But Molai shows how sustained planting with native species, over decades, can turn bare ground into habitat, and how local knowledge of wildlife and neighbours is part of the work.
setbacks: Al Jazeera reported that elephants from the forest damaged crops in nearby villages and some villagers threatened to destroy it; Payeng responded by planting more banana trees. In late 2025 a fire attributed by officials to arson destroyed thousands of saplings in a newer planted section.

copy_this.problem: Bare, eroded or degraded land near where you live.
copy_this.what: Plant and, above all, keep tending native species suited to the site, starting small and expanding over years.
copy_this.materials: Locally sourced native seedlings or cuttings, simple hand tools, water access, protection from grazing.
copy_this.skills: Knowledge of local plants and soils; advice from foresters or local elders helps.
copy_this.time: Years to decades of regular care.
copy_this.people: One person can start; landholders and neighbours must agree.
copy_this.risks: Planting on land you do not have permission to use; choosing invasive species; wildlife conflict with neighbouring farms; fire.
copy_this.adapt: Smaller versions work as school woodlands, hedgerows or riverbank planting.
copy_this.lessons: Native species and patience matter more than numbers planted; involve neighbours early to avoid conflict.

title: Slowing meltwater to store ice for spring sowing in Ladakh
person: Chewang Norphel
status_note: A 2024 interview (ETV Bharat, October 2024) described Norphel as 89 and still speaking about the work. Sources give the first ice reservoir as 1986 or 1987. In 2018 he said he hoped younger people would take the work on.
summary: Retired engineer Chewang Norphel builds low-cost 'artificial glaciers' that freeze winter stream water near Ladakhi villages so it melts in time for spring sowing.
small_thing: Norphel noticed that a tap left running near his home through winter built up a large block of ice, while a fast-flowing stream nearby never froze. He reasoned that slowing water down would make it freeze.
problem_text: Farming in Ladakh's cold desert depends on meltwater. Natural glaciers lie far above villages and melt mostly from June, after crops need to be sown, and many nearby glaciers have shrunk. Winter stream water, meanwhile, simply flows away.
why_started: Norphel, a Ladakhi civil engineer with the Jammu and Kashmir Rural Development Department, saw water shortages at sowing time in villages such as Phuktse. He told Scientific American that water is the region's most precious commodity and that disputes over it divide families.
what_they_did:
In the mid-1980s Norphel built his first ice reservoir at Phuktse. Villagers divert a stream in autumn into shallow, stepped basins held back by stone embankments, often on shaded slopes. Keeping the water only a few inches deep and slowing its flow lets it freeze layer by layer through winter, close to the village and at a lower altitude.

The ice melts earlier than natural glaciers, releasing water in April and May for sowing. According to IANS (2018) he had built 17 such structures; ETV Bharat (2024) reports at least 15. IANS reported the first cost about Rs 90,000.
what_changed: A peer-reviewed study led by Heidelberg University (Nüsser et al., 2018) estimated typical ice reservoirs store about 1,010 to 3,220 cubic metres of water and found that, in the best case, fields could be fully irrigated up to three times; local smallholders reported less risk of crop failure. Norphel received the Padma Shri in 2015 (IANS).
what_they_learned: Norphel describes the method simply as harvesting winter water that would otherwise be wasted, in the form of ice, and stresses that slowing the water is the key.

quote.text: It's a technique to harvest winter waste water in the form of ice.

why_it_matters: Ice reservoirs cannot replace shrinking natural glaciers. But they show how a simple, locally built structure can shift when water is available, and how adaptation can grow from close observation of local conditions.
setbacks: The Heidelberg study found storage varies from year to year with weather, that floods, landslides and avalanches reduce effectiveness, and that the reservoirs are not always well integrated into local social arrangements; it described the term 'artificial glacier' as misleading. ETV Bharat reported that seepage into the ground can account for a large share of losses during construction.

copy_this.problem: Water arriving at the wrong time of year for crops.
copy_this.what: Look for ways to store seasonal surplus water near where it is needed: ponds, tanks, ice basins in cold climates, or soil-moisture measures.
copy_this.materials: Depends on climate: stone, earth and pipes for diversion channels; local building materials.
copy_this.skills: Basic engineering or hydrology advice; knowledge of local water rights and seasons.
copy_this.time: A season to build; yearly maintenance.
copy_this.people: A whole village or water-user group.
copy_this.risks: Diverting water can affect downstream users and requires agreement; poorly built structures can fail in floods.
copy_this.adapt: In warmer regions the same idea applies to rainwater harvesting and check dams.
copy_this.lessons: Observe local conditions closely; agree water sharing before building; measure whether it actually helps.

title: If children can't reach school, the school comes by boat
person: Mohammed Rezwan (Shidhulai Swanirvar Sangstha)
status_note: Reuters reported in October 2025 that 26 boat schools were operating with 2,240 pupils enrolled.
summary: Architect Mohammed Rezwan founded Shidhulai Swanirvar Sangstha, which runs solar-powered boats serving as schools, libraries and clinics for flood-prone villages in north-west Bangladesh.
small_thing: As a young architecture graduate, Rezwan used his scholarship money and savings to found a small organisation in 1998, and spent four years raising funds for a first school boat.
problem_text: In the Chalan Beel wetland of north-west Bangladesh, the area under water expands greatly in the monsoon. Roads are scarce, schools flood, and children in riverside villages can be cut off from classes for months.
why_started: Rezwan told Down To Earth: "I thought if children cannot go to schools then schools should come to children." He founded the organisation to test that idea in his home area.
what_they_did:
The first school boat was built in 2002, made with local boat builders using local timber. Boats collect children from riverside villages, then moor to hold lessons, with solar panels on the roof powering lights and computers. The organisation added boat libraries, clinics, farmer training centres and flood shelters.

Shidhulai also distributed solar lanterns and small solar home systems. According to Ashden, solar lanterns let fishers work at night and replaced kerosene lamps.
what_changed: Ashden, which gave Shidhulai an award in 2007, reported 88 boats and about 87,000 families benefiting at that time. Reuters reported in 2025 that the model had expanded to more than 100 boats serving as schools, libraries and clinics, that 26 boat schools had 2,240 pupils enrolled, and that more than 22,000 students had been educated. These figures come from the organisation via Ashden and Reuters.
what_they_learned: Rezwan has described involving the local community and paying staff properly as essential to building trust. He also had to work directly with boat builders who could not read architectural drawings.

quote.text: I thought if children cannot go to schools then schools should come to children.

why_it_matters: Boat schools do not stop flooding. But they show a practical way to keep services running where water levels rise, combining local craft skills with small-scale solar power.
setbacks: Down To Earth reported that raising money for the first boat took four years and that local boat builders could not follow Rezwan's drawings, so he worked with them directly.

copy_this.problem: Essential services cut off by seasonal flooding or poor transport.
copy_this.what: Bring the service to people: mobile classrooms, libraries or clinics using transport that suits local conditions.
copy_this.materials: Locally built vehicles or boats, small solar panels and batteries, books or learning materials.
copy_this.skills: Local building skills, teaching or health staff, basic solar maintenance, fundraising.
copy_this.time: Years to establish; ongoing operation.
copy_this.people: A small team, trained local staff and community support.
copy_this.risks: Safety on water; dependence on donor funding; maintaining equipment.
copy_this.adapt: Mobile libraries or solar-charging stations can start on a much smaller scale.
copy_this.lessons: Design with local builders and residents; small solar systems can make a large difference off-grid.

title: Two schoolgirls ask Bali to say goodbye to plastic bags
person: Melati and Isabel Wijsen
status_note: Bali's single-use plastic regulation (Governor Regulation No. 97/2018) was upheld by Indonesia's Supreme Court in 2019. ADB reported in 2021 that Bye Bye Plastic Bags continued clean-ups and education; Melati Wijsen also founded YOUTHTOPIA.
summary: Sisters Melati and Isabel Wijsen started Bye Bye Plastic Bags in Bali in 2013, campaigning with petitions and clean-ups until the province restricted single-use plastic.
small_thing: After a school lesson about change-makers such as Nelson Mandela and Mahatma Gandhi, the young sisters decided to start a campaign against plastic bags on their island.
problem_text: Plastic bags littered Bali's beaches and waterways, wrapping around swimmers at the sisters' childhood beach. Isabel Wijsen told audiences that very little of this plastic was recycled.
why_started: According to NPR, the sisters were inspired by a school lesson on significant people who changed the world, and decided they did not need to wait until they were older. Seeing plastic on the beaches they grew up on gave them their cause.
what_they_did:
The sisters founded Bye Bye Plastic Bags in 2013. They ran an online petition, beach clean-ups and workshops in schools and communities. Inspired by Gandhi, they announced a food strike; NPR reported that within a day the then governor invited them to his office and signed a memorandum of understanding to work towards reducing plastic.

The group later started Mountain Mamas, a social enterprise in which village women make reusable bags, and organised annual island-wide clean-ups.
what_changed: The governor's promise of a plastic-bag-free Bali by 2018 was missed. In December 2018 the new governor issued Regulation No. 97/2018 limiting single-use plastics, which Indonesia's Supreme Court upheld in 2019 after a challenge by recyclers and businessmen (The Jakarta Post). The ban followed years of pressure from many groups; the sisters' campaign was one widely reported part. According to the Asian Development Bank, their annual clean-ups had mobilised over 60,000 people and kept over 130 tonnes of plastic from the ocean over five years (the organisation's figures).
what_they_learned: Melati has described working with politicians as slow and uneven, likening it to taking three steps forward and two steps back, again and again.

quote.text: Don't ever let anyone tell you that you're too young or you won't understand.
quote.speaker: Isabel Wijsen

why_it_matters: A regional bag ban does not end plastic pollution, and enforcement is a separate challenge. But this campaign shows how young people can use petitions, persistence and public attention to move a policy debate.
setbacks: The original 2018 deadline promised by the governor was not met, and the sisters had to keep pressing officials at several levels. The eventual regulation faced a legal challenge from a recyclers' association before being upheld.

copy_this.problem: Single-use plastic in your school, market or town.
copy_this.what: Start with a clear, specific ask (such as ending free plastic bags), then combine clean-ups, a petition and talks with decision-makers.
copy_this.materials: Petition platform or paper forms, clean-up kit, simple information materials.
copy_this.skills: Public speaking, organising, patience with officials.
copy_this.time: Months to years.
copy_this.people: A small core group with wider supporters.
copy_this.risks: Young campaigners need adult support and safeguarding; avoid protest tactics that put health at risk.
copy_this.adapt: Can target a single school canteen, market or local council.
copy_this.lessons: Policy takes persistence; offer alternatives such as reusable bags alongside the ask.

title: A mountain town that sorts its rubbish into 45 categories
person: Residents of Kamikatsu
status_note: The town missed its goal of zero waste by 2020 and has set a new plan running to 2030.
occupation: Residents, town government and the non-profit Zero Waste Academy
summary: Kamikatsu, a small town in Tokushima, declared Japan's first zero-waste goal in 2003; residents wash, sort and bring their waste to a central station.
small_thing: Residents began washing their food packaging and carrying their own rubbish, sorted by type, to the town's collection centre instead of having it burned.
problem_text: Kamikatsu, a mountain town on Shikoku with fewer than 1,500 residents, used to burn its rubbish in the open. Stricter rules forced it to stop, and its small incinerators were closed in 2001, leaving it to find another way to deal with waste.
why_started: With open burning no longer allowed and incineration ended, the town expanded the sorting it had begun in 1997. In 2003 it became the first municipality in Japan to declare a zero-waste goal.
what_they_did:
There is no household rubbish collection. Most residents take washed and sorted waste to the town's collection station, where it is divided into 45 categories (paper alone has several). A truck collects from elderly residents who cannot drive.

The town opened a reuse shop, Kurukuru, where people leave and take items free of charge, and a workshop that remakes old textiles. A Zero Waste Center opened in 2020. The non-profit Zero Waste Academy helps run the programme and certifies local businesses that cut waste.
what_changed: Nippon.com reported a recycling rate of about 80% in 2021, against a Japanese national average of about 20%. WHYY reported that the town's zero-waste coordinator said recycling cost far less than incinerating everything. The town did not reach zero waste by 2020, and says the remaining fifth of its waste cannot be solved by residents alone.
what_they_learned: The town concluded that consumers alone cannot eliminate the last 20% of waste, and that business partnerships and product design must change too. Residents say sorting becomes habit once established, but some newcomers find it confusing and time-consuming.

quote.text: Once custom is changed, it becomes habit
quote.speaker: Akira Sakano, Zero Waste Academy

why_it_matters: Kamikatsu is small, and its model asks a lot of residents. But it shows that careful sorting, reuse and local facilities can divert most household waste from burning, and it highlights where manufacturers and retailers need to act.
setbacks: The 2020 zero-waste goal was missed. Washing and drying packaging is seen as a burden by many residents, newcomers struggle with the system, and population decline is an added challenge (Nippon.com; WHYY).

copy_this.problem: Mixed household rubbish going to landfill or incineration.
copy_this.what: Start a shared sorting point or a free swap shelf for your street, building, school or village.
copy_this.materials: Labelled bins, a sheltered space, clear signage, a shelf or room for swaps.
copy_this.skills: Organising, knowing which local recyclers accept which materials.
copy_this.time: A few weeks to set up; regular upkeep.
copy_this.people: A few volunteers plus the cooperation of households.
copy_this.risks: Sorted material is wasted if no recycler will take it; check with your council or waste company first.
copy_this.adapt: Begin with three or four categories and add more as people get used to it.
copy_this.lessons: Make it easy and explain why; some waste can only be avoided by changes upstream.

title: Law students in Vanuatu take climate change to the World Court
person: Pacific Islands Students Fighting Climate Change
status_note: The International Court of Justice delivered its advisory opinion on 23 July 2025. In 2026 the group was working on implementation, noting the opinion is not self-executing.
summary: In 2019, 27 law students at the University of the South Pacific began a campaign that led to the International Court of Justice's 2025 advisory opinion on climate change.
small_thing: After a law class in 2019, 27 students asked why international climate rules were so weak and decided to campaign for the world's highest court to be asked what states owe.
problem_text: Pacific island nations contribute little to global emissions but face sea-level rise, stronger storms and other climate harms. Climate commitments under international agreements have largely been voluntary pledges.
why_started: According to Right Livelihood, the students began after a 2019 law lecture that left them questioning the weakness of international climate regimes. Founding member Vishal Prasad told Amnesty International that the students knew the cost of the climate crisis to their region well.
what_they_did:
The students drafted a question on states' obligations to present and future generations and pressed Pacific governments to take it up. Vanuatu's government adopted the proposal, and in March 2023 the UN General Assembly asked the Court for an advisory opinion by consensus.

The group built a youth network and a civil society alliance, gathered testimony from communities in the Solomon Islands, Fiji and Tonga, and in December 2024 members addressed the Court at its hearings in The Hague.
what_changed: On 23 July 2025 the International Court of Justice unanimously delivered an advisory opinion stating that states have obligations under climate treaties, human rights law and customary international law to prevent climate harm, and that breaches can carry legal consequences (Right Livelihood; Amnesty; PINA). Advisory opinions are not legally binding but carry significant authority. In 2025 the group shared the Right Livelihood Award with Julian Aguon.
what_they_learned: Prasad has said the campaign began with no budget, office or recognition, and that the ruling only has force where people insist on it.

quote.text: For the first time, the law says states can't just promise. They are obliged,
quote.speaker: Vishal Prasad, PISFCC director

why_it_matters: A court opinion does not cut emissions by itself, and its effect depends on governments and courts using it. But this case shows how a small group of students, working with their government, used international law to put the concerns of vulnerable communities before the world's highest court.
setbacks: The campaign started with no funding or standing. The opinion is advisory rather than binding, and campaigners say turning it into action now depends on governments (PINA, 2026).

copy_this.problem: Decision-makers not acting on a local environmental harm.
copy_this.what: Use existing legal and democratic routes: research the rules, frame a clear question, and ask representatives to raise it formally.
copy_this.materials: Access to legal information, a clear written brief, a way to gather community testimony.
copy_this.skills: Research, writing, advocacy; advice from qualified lawyers.
copy_this.time: Years.
copy_this.people: A committed core group plus allies and partner organisations.
copy_this.risks: Legal processes are slow; seek proper legal advice and get informed consent before sharing people's stories.
copy_this.adapt: At local level, the same approach applies to petitions, planning objections or freedom of information requests.
copy_this.lessons: Start with a precise question; build broad alliances; a legal win needs follow-up to make a difference.

title: Catching fog for water above Lima's hillside settlements
person: Abel Cruz Gutiérrez
status_note: Started year reflects Guernica's report that Cruz joined a fog-water pilot in 2006; in a 2024 first-person account (Orato) he says he founded his movement in 2002. Still active as of that 2024 report.
occupation: Industrial engineer (as described by Orato); founder of the Movimiento Peruanos Sin Agua
summary: Abel Cruz and his movement put up nylon mesh nets on the hills around Lima to catch coastal fog, giving water-poor settlements a small, local supply.
small_thing: By his own account, Cruz noticed that the plastic mesh fencing around his home on the edge of Lima was collecting droplets of moisture from the fog. He began experimenting with mesh as a way of catching water.
problem_text: Lima sits in a desert and receives almost no rain. Around a million residents, many in hillside settlements, have no piped water and buy it from tanker trucks at prices well above what connected households pay. Reporting in 2012 noted that the water utility did not expect to reach some of these hills soon.
why_started: After years of protesting for fairer access to city water, Cruz turned to building a supply communities could make themselves; he told Guernica they had never stopped to think about making their own. He grew up hauling water uphill near Cusco, an experience he links to his work.
what_they_did:
Cruz took part in a fog-water pilot when the German group Alimón e.V. came to Peru in 2006, helping with pilot studies, choosing sites and training residents to build the nets. Each net is a sheet of nylon mesh about 6 by 4 metres, strung on hillsides where fog drifts in from the Pacific; droplets collect on the mesh and run into tanks.

In Cerro Nueva Esperanza, on Lima's outskirts, Al Jazeera reported in 2012 that 20 nets fed a system of plastic tubes and 20 tanks. Cruz secured a USAID grant to build more nets and says he has since installed many more.
what_changed: According to Al Jazeera (2012), each net in Cerro Nueva Esperanza could condense about 90 litres a day, up to about 3,000 litres in total on good days, and more than 70 families received water in their taps; one resident used it to grow a garden. In a 2024 interview with Orato, Cruz said he had installed around 6,000 fog catchers, a figure that has not been independently verified. Both sources note the water is used mainly for irrigation and cleaning rather than drinking.
what_they_learned: Cruz has said the nets work best as a supplement, and that the water still needs treatment before drinking; he is researching natural purification methods. He also describes patience: his first trial produced nothing for eight days.

quote.text: this could become the pilot programme to secure water for thousands of people
quote.speaker: Abel Cruz

why_it_matters: Fog nets cannot supply a city of millions, and reporters have stressed they meet only a small share of need. But they show how a low-tech, locally built device can ease daily water costs for households left off the network, and how a community can make use of a resource that is otherwise ignored.
setbacks: The water is not yet safe to drink without treatment. Output depends heavily on fog density and season. Journalists have noted that the scale is far too small to meet Lima's water needs, which still require public investment.

copy_this.problem: Households in dry, foggy places with little or no piped water.
copy_this.what: Mesh nets on frames placed on slopes where fog regularly passes, with gutters and pipes leading to storage tanks.
copy_this.materials: Fine mesh (such as nylon or polypropylene), poles, cables, gutters, pipes, covered tanks.
copy_this.skills: Basic construction; site selection with local knowledge of fog patterns; water-quality testing.
copy_this.time: Weeks to install; a season of monitoring to see yield.
copy_this.people: A small team plus households who will maintain it.
copy_this.risks: Water may be contaminated; use for irrigation or cleaning unless it is tested and treated. Steep sites can be dangerous to work on; secure frames against wind.
copy_this.adapt: Only suitable where fog is frequent; check with local water or meteorological services first.
copy_this.lessons: Measure yield before scaling up, and treat fog water as a supplement rather than a full supply.

title: A young Anishinaabe water protector speaks up for clean water
person: Autumn Peltier
city: Wiikwemkoong Unceded Territory, Manitoulin Island, Ontario
status_note: Start year is approximate: the Canadian Museum of History says her activism began at age eight, and she was 12 in 2016. A 2026 conference biography describes her as 21 and still working as an activist and UN ambassador and contributor.
occupation: Water-rights advocate; Anishinabek Nation Chief Water Commissioner (as described in 2022)
summary: Inspired by boil-water notices she saw as a child, Autumn Peltier has spent her youth calling on leaders to protect water and guarantee safe drinking water for First Nations.
small_thing: At about eight years old she attended a ceremony at Serpent River First Nation and noticed signs warning people to boil their water. Asking why became the start of her advocacy.
problem_text: Many First Nations communities in Canada have lived under long-term drinking-water advisories, meaning tap water is unsafe without boiling. Pipelines and pollution also raise concerns about the lakes and rivers that communities depend on.
why_started: According to the Canadian Museum of History, the boil-water signs at Serpent River First Nation inspired her to fight for safe drinking water on reserves and elsewhere. Her activism draws on teachings from her mother and her great-aunt Josephine Mandamin, a well-known Indigenous water activist in the Great Lakes region.
what_they_did:
In 2016, aged 12, she spoke directly to Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, asking him to protect the waters from pipeline development. In March 2018, at 13, she addressed the UN General Assembly at the launch of the International Decade for Action on water, urging leaders to 'warrior up' and arguing that water should have rights and protection.

After Josephine Mandamin died in 2019, the Anishinabek Nation chose Peltier as its Chief Water Commissioner. She has continued to speak at international events.
what_changed: Her advocacy is about awareness and pressure rather than measurable outputs, and its policy effects have not been independently measured. Her standing is reflected in institutional recognition: the Canadian Museum of History displayed objects from her work, including the dress she wore at the UN, in 2022–23, and she was a finalist for the International Children's Peace Prize in 2022, the first Canadian to reach that stage.
what_they_learned: Peltier has framed water as something living that deserves rights and protection, and has stressed that clean water should be available to everyone, not just those who can afford it.

quote.text: Our water deserves to be treated as human with human rights.

why_it_matters: One young person's speeches will not fix water infrastructure. But her story shows how a child's question, backed by family and community teaching, can keep a long-standing injustice in public view and bring Indigenous understandings of water into international discussion.

copy_this.problem: An environmental injustice in your community that decision-makers are not addressing.
copy_this.what: Learn the facts, learn from elders and local knowledge holders, and speak to decision-makers in public and in person.
copy_this.materials: Reliable information, a clear message, a platform such as a school, community meeting or local media.
copy_this.skills: Public speaking, listening, research.
copy_this.time: Ongoing; years for lasting change.
copy_this.people: One person can start, ideally with family or community support.
copy_this.risks: Public attention can be stressful, especially for young people; involve trusted adults and protect personal details online.
copy_this.adapt: Root your message in your own community's experience and, where relevant, Indigenous protocols and leadership.
copy_this.lessons: Personal, first-hand stories tied to a clear ask carry weight with leaders.

title: The Amsterdam meet-up that made repair social again
person: Martine Postma
status_note: Postma was campaigning for repair policy as of a January 2025 report. Sources differ on when the Repair Café Foundation began (2010 per AFP and the Christian Science Monitor; the foundation says it has supported local groups since 2011).
occupation: Former journalist; founder of the Repair Café Foundation
summary: In 2009 Martine Postma held a free repair meet-up in Amsterdam. The idea of volunteers helping neighbours fix broken things has since spread to thousands of Repair Cafés worldwide.
small_thing: On 18 October 2009 she organised a single afternoon in Amsterdam where volunteers with repair skills helped people fix broken items for free.
problem_text: Many household items are thrown away when they could be fixed, often because people do not know how to repair them or cannot find parts and information. This adds to waste and the demand for new products.
why_started: Postma was a journalist writing about sustainability and waste. After covering an exhibition on repair in 2009, she told iFixit she wanted to do more than just write about it. She told AFP that people had lost the culture of repair.
what_they_did:
The first Repair Café brought together volunteers with tools and skills and visitors bringing broken household items, with repairs done together so visitors learn as well. Its success led Postma to set up a foundation that offers a starter kit and advice so others can run their own events.

The foundation, which received Dutch government support in its early years, has also pushed for repair-friendly policy. The Christian Science Monitor reports that Postma and the foundation played a key role in the EU's 2024 right-to-repair directive, whose legal text mentions Repair Cafés.
what_changed: AFP reported about 20 Repair Cafés in the Netherlands by March 2012. By January 2025, the Christian Science Monitor reported nearly 3,200 in more than 40 countries, and cited the foundation's annual report as saying Repair Cafés kept over 1.4 million pounds of broken goods out of landfill in 2023. These waste figures come from the organisation's own reporting.
what_they_learned: Postma has observed that many items brought in are not truly broken and only need cleaning or small fixes, and that people discard things because they do not know what else to do, not because they want to.

quote.text: People have simply lost the culture of repairs.

why_it_matters: A monthly repair session will not change how products are designed. But Repair Cafés keep usable goods in circulation, pass on practical skills, and have given policymakers visible evidence that people want things that can be fixed.
setbacks: Manufacturers initially distanced themselves, saying amateur repair was dangerous. Postma notes that the EU directive covers only a limited range of products, and that parts and repair information remain hard to obtain.

copy_this.problem: Usable items being thrown away for lack of repair skills.
copy_this.what: A regular free repair session where volunteers fix items alongside their owners.
copy_this.materials: A community venue, tables, basic tools, sewing kit, multimeter, safety equipment, tea and coffee.
copy_this.skills: Volunteers with sewing, electrical, mechanical or bike repair skills; an organiser.
copy_this.time: A few weeks to plan; a half-day session each month.
copy_this.people: An organiser plus a handful of volunteer fixers.
copy_this.risks: Electrical safety; agree clear house rules and check whether you need public liability insurance.
copy_this.adapt: Start with the skills your volunteers already have; link with local libraries or schools.
copy_this.lessons: Repairing with the owner, rather than for them, builds skills and confidence.

title: Planting vegetables in public spaces across a Pennine town
person: Pam Warhurst and Mary Clear (co-founders), with volunteers of Incredible Edible Todmorden
status_note: Pam Warhurst was giving talks about the project in January 2026. No 2024–2026 news on Mary Clear's current role was found. The project describes itself as having no office, paid staff or major funding.
occupation: Volunteers; Pam Warhurst has been described as a community leader and Mary Clear as a gardener (as documented)
summary: Volunteers in Todmorden began planting herbs, fruit and vegetables in public spaces for anyone to pick, sparking a wider Incredible Edible movement.
small_thing: Mary Clear planted vegetables in her front garden and put up a sign inviting passers-by to help themselves. Volunteers then began planting herbs and vegetables on neglected verges and outside public buildings.
problem_text: Many towns depend on long supply chains for food, and many people have little connection to where it comes from or space to grow it. Todmorden's founders also saw a town divided by its main roads, with few shared spaces bringing residents together.
why_started: The founders believed growing food in public could bring people together and make the town more connected and resilient (organisation's own account). The Ecologist reported their aim of reducing dependence on global supply chains, under the motto 'If you eat, you're in'.
what_they_did:
Starting in 2008 with a public meeting of about sixty people, volunteers planted food at public sites including the police station, the health centre, the canal towpath and the railway station, often without waiting for formal permission. They called some plots 'propaganda gardens' to start conversations about local, seasonal food.

The group worked with schools, a housing association and a care home on growing spaces, created a walking route of edible plantings, and supported local farmers and food businesses. A National Lottery grant of more than £500,000 later funded projects including an aquaponics unit at the high school.
what_changed: Writing in Farming Matters in 2011, John Paull reported food planted at about forty public sites in a town of around 17,000 people, with all local schools growing food. The Ecologist (2014) reported a thousand-tree orchard and about 50 Incredible Edible groups across the UK. A Hebden Bridge news report in January 2026 put the wider network at more than 200 UK groups and about 1,000 worldwide; the project's own site says over 700. These counts are not independently audited, and the effect on local food security has not been measured.
what_they_learned: The group says small, consistent actions had the most impact and that some early ideas did not work. Paull noted that the idea of picking food someone else had planted took about two years to catch on.

quote.text: We don't ask permission. It takes too long and anyway we're improving the place.
quote.speaker: Pam Warhurst

why_it_matters: Herb beds at a bus stop will not feed a town. But Todmorden showed how unused public land can become a shared resource, and how visible growing can reconnect people with food and with each other at very low cost.
setbacks: The idea of taking food from public beds was slow to be accepted, taking around two years to catch on according to Paull. The group says some early ideas did not thrive, and it runs without paid staff or core funding.

copy_this.problem: Little connection between residents and local food; unused public land.
copy_this.what: Plant herbs, fruit and vegetables in visible public spots with signs inviting people to pick.
copy_this.materials: Planters or raised beds, compost, seeds and plants, signs, watering cans.
copy_this.skills: Basic gardening; talking to neighbours and landowners.
copy_this.time: One afternoon to plant a first bed; ongoing weekly care.
copy_this.people: A few committed volunteers to start.
copy_this.risks: Check soil for contamination on old urban sites and avoid planting beside busy roads; agree access with the landowner or council where needed.
copy_this.adapt: Choose hardy crops suited to your climate; partner with schools, housing providers and care homes.
copy_this.lessons: Start small and visible; consistent care matters more than big plans.

title: Mayan beekeepers take the fight for their honey to Mexico's Supreme Court
person: Leydy Pech
status_note: Beekeeping work with Mayan women predates the 2012 legal campaign. Most recent independent profile found is from November 2023 (Latin America Bureau); no 2024–2026 news on her personally was found.
occupation: Beekeeper; member of the Mayan women's cooperative Koolel-Kab/Muuchkambal
summary: Mayan beekeeper Leydy Pech built a coalition that challenged genetically modified soy permits in court, defending native bees, honey livelihoods and Indigenous communities' right to be consulted.
small_thing: With other Mayan women in Hopelchén, she helped revive the keeping of the native stingless bee Melipona beecheii, known locally as Xunáan Kab.
problem_text: Honey is a vital income for Mayan families on the Yucatán Peninsula. In 2012 Mexico's government permitted Monsanto to plant herbicide-tolerant GM soy in seven states, including Campeche, without consulting local communities. Researchers later found GM soy pollen in Campeche honey and glyphosate in Hopelchén's water.
why_started: According to the Goldman Environmental Prize, the GM soy permits threatened local honey, the environment and livelihoods, and Indigenous communities had not been consulted. Pech described the campaign as a struggle for life.
what_they_did:
In June 2012 Pech formed the coalition Sin Transgénicos, bringing together beekeepers, NGOs and environmentalists, and that month sued the Mexican government, arguing that failing to consult Indigenous communities breached Mexico's Constitution and ILO Convention 169.

She worked with universities to gather evidence on pollen in honey and glyphosate in water, and the coalition ran workshops, petitions and simultaneous protests at seven Mayan ceremonial sites.
what_changed: According to the Goldman Prize, Mexico's Supreme Court ruled unanimously in November 2015 that Indigenous communities must be consulted before GM soy is planted, which effectively cancelled the permits in Campeche and Yucatán. In September 2017 the national agricultural health service revoked Monsanto's permits in seven states. Latin America Bureau reported in 2023 that illegal soy planting and fumigation continued and that consultation processes had stalled.
what_they_learned: Pech's campaign relied on combining Indigenous rights law with scientific evidence and broad community organising, according to accounts by the Goldman Prize and Latin America Bureau.
why_it_matters: A court ruling did not end pressure on the region's forests and bees, and enforcement has been weak. But the case set a precedent that Indigenous communities must be consulted before such crops are planted, and showed how small-scale producers can defend both their livelihoods and biodiversity through the law.
setbacks: She faced discrimination and threats. Latin America Bureau reported that illegal GM soy planting and fumigation continued after the ruling, and that disputes over land use with large-scale agriculture persist.

copy_this.problem: Local farming or beekeeping livelihoods threatened by decisions taken without community consultation.
copy_this.what: Build a coalition of producers and allies, gather independent evidence, and use consultation and rights law.
copy_this.materials: Records of local impacts, links with universities or labs, legal advice.
copy_this.skills: Community organising, partnership with researchers, legal support.
copy_this.time: Years.
copy_this.people: A coalition of producers, NGOs and lawyers.
copy_this.risks: Campaigners can face threats; plan for safety and seek support from human rights organisations.
copy_this.adapt: Use the consultation laws and rights that apply in your own country.
copy_this.lessons: Independent scientific evidence strengthens community legal claims.

title: Bogotá's waste pickers organise to be paid for recycling
person: Nohra Padilla
status_note: Most recent source found (Bogotá city government, May 2022) describes her as a member of the Asociación de Recicladores de Bogotá working on a plastic-wood venture. No 2024–2026 news was found.
occupation: Recycler (waste picker); executive director of the Asociación de Recicladores de Bogotá (as reported in 2016)
summary: A third-generation waste picker, Nohra Padilla helped organise Bogotá's recyclers and won legal recognition and payment for their work in the city's waste system.
small_thing: She began recycling alongside her family at the age of seven, and later joined fellow recyclers in forming cooperatives to protect their right to keep working.
problem_text: Informal recyclers recover much of a city's reusable material but have often been excluded, harassed and poorly paid. In Bogotá, plans to privatise waste collection threatened to shut them out of the work altogether.
why_started: When the dump that supported her community closed, recyclers had to search the streets, where they faced harassment. Padilla told the Goldman Prize that their goal was to improve working and living conditions for recyclers.
what_they_did:
In 1990 Padilla helped set up the Asociación de Recicladores de Bogotá, which grew to represent about 3,000 recyclers, and helped build a national association. Recyclers ran their own collection centres and campaigned for recognition.

She filed the legal challenge that led Colombia's Constitutional Court in December 2011 to cancel a large tender that would have handed recycling to private companies, ordering that waste pickers be included in the system.
what_changed: According to the Goldman Prize and WIEGO, Bogotá's mayor then made recycling mandatory and created payment for recyclers' services, and recyclers became formal participants in city waste planning, with uniforms and identity cards. WIEGO reported that 790 waste pickers and their families could see their earnings double or triple. Later outcomes across the city have not been independently measured.
what_they_learned: Padilla has said that waste pickers have been invisible everywhere and that change only came once they organised, and that access to waste is the key to protecting their work.

quote.text: Becoming organized is a difficult process. In every country in the world, waste pickers have been invisible

why_it_matters: Paying recyclers does not by itself solve a city's waste problem. But Bogotá's experience shows that recognising the people already doing the work can make recycling fairer and more dependable, and it has been cited as a model by waste-picker organisations elsewhere.
setbacks: She faced threats and false accusations, was jailed for eight days before being acquitted, and was refused state protection. Thousands of recyclers elsewhere in Colombia were still outside payment schemes, according to WIEGO.

copy_this.problem: Informal recyclers excluded from formal waste systems.
copy_this.what: Support recyclers to organise into associations and push for recognition, fair contracts and payment.
copy_this.materials: Meeting space, records of material collected, legal advice.
copy_this.skills: Organising, negotiation, knowledge of local waste law.
copy_this.time: Years.
copy_this.people: Recyclers themselves, with allies in civil society.
copy_this.risks: Organisers can face hostility from vested interests; prioritise safety and alliances.
copy_this.adapt: Residents can help locally by separating recyclables and supporting recycler cooperatives.
copy_this.lessons: Change came when recyclers organised and claimed a formal role.
